0.title: Whole in Christ, at Home in His Family
0.essay:
This study is for single Christians of every age and every story: the never-married student and the never-married pensioner, the widow and the widower, the divorced and the separated, the single parent, and the believer who has chosen a single life for Christ’s sake. It is also for the churches they belong to, because singleness is never only a private matter. It is a question about what the family of God is for.

A quiet assumption

Many churches carry a quiet assumption that the normal Christian life is a married one, and that single people are waiting for theirs to begin. Scripture does not share it. The Son of God lived his whole earthly life unmarried. So, when he wrote his letters, did the apostle Paul. Neither was half a person, and neither lived half a life.

Honest and hopeful

Yet this study will not pretend that singleness is always easy. Many single people did not choose it. Some long for marriage and children. Some have lost a husband or wife to death, or to unfaithfulness. Loneliness can be sharp, and sexual faithfulness can be hard. The Bible does not hurry past these things. It gives words for lament, grace for weakness, a family for the solitary, and a hope in which every human marriage gives way to the marriage of the Lamb.

Other studies in this commentary touch on singleness: Christian Marriage, Biblical Sexuality, Divorce & Remarriage, Friendship & Hospitality and Faith for Young Adults. This one gathers the theme together and speaks to single readers directly.

The chapters

Single Like Our Lord; A Gift, Not a Rank; Longing, Loneliness and Lament; Faithful in Body, Content in Heart; Widowed and Single Again; and A Family Now, a Wedding to Come.

For reflection

Whether you are single or married, what have you assumed, perhaps without noticing, about what makes a life full?

1.title: Single Like Our Lord
1.essay:
“And the Word became flesh and dwelt among us” (John 1:14). The eternal Son took a real human life, and he lived it, from the manger to the cross, as an unmarried man. That simple fact changes how every single Christian may see himself or herself.

Many ways of being single

“Single” covers many lives. A woman of twenty-six who hopes to marry. A man of fifty-eight who never did. A widow of eighty who was married for half a century. A father raising two children after his wife left. A believer who is attracted to the same sex and has chosen, for Christ’s sake, not to pursue a sexual relationship. A missionary who decided long ago that a single life would serve the work best. Their joys and sorrows differ. But Scripture speaks to all of them, and it begins with Jesus.

The single Saviour

Jesus was fully human. He ate, slept, worked, wept and was tempted “in every respect” as we are, yet without sin (Hebrews 4:15). And he never married. If marriage were necessary to a complete human life, then the life of the only perfect man would have been incomplete. It was not. He was the most whole human being who has ever lived.

His single life was not a lonely one in the sense of being loveless. He had close friends. At the grave of Lazarus, “Jesus wept. So the Jews said, ‘See how he loved him!’” (John 11:35–36). Yet he also knew the cost of his path. “Foxes have holes, and birds of the air have nests, but the Son of Man has nowhere to lay his head” (Matthew 8:20). No home of his own, no wife waiting, no children to carry his name. He understands.

Paul and others

Paul wrote to the unmarried and widows that it is good for them “to remain single, as I am” (1 Corinthians 7:8). Whether he had once been married, Scripture does not say. He knew he had “the right to take along a believing wife” (1 Corinthians 9:5), as other apostles did, and he chose not to use it for the sake of the gospel.

Scripture shows others too. God told Jeremiah not to take a wife (Jeremiah 16:2), so that his empty house would be a living warning to a nation heading for disaster. Philip the evangelist “had four unmarried daughters, who prophesied” (Acts 21:9). In later centuries many fruitful servants of Christ, such as Charles Simeon, Amy Carmichael and John Stott, never married. Singleness has never kept anyone out of the centre of God’s purposes.

Filled in him

The deepest reason a single Christian is not incomplete is union with Christ. “For in him the whole fullness of deity dwells bodily, and you have been filled in him” (Colossians 2:9–10). Every believer, married or single, has been joined to the one in whom all the fullness of God lives. Nothing essential is missing.

And the love at the centre of every Christian life is already yours. Paul did not write of a love he hoped one day to find, but of “the Son of God, who loved me and gave himself for me” (Galatians 2:20). No husband or wife could ever love you more deeply, or more faithfully, than the one who died for you. Your life “is hidden with Christ in God” (Colossians 3:3), and it is safe there.

Names that are not yours

Single people are often given names, spoken or unspoken: left on the shelf, a failed marriage, incomplete, too fussy, not yet a real adult. In Isaiah’s day the eunuch, who could never have children, was tempted to say, “Behold, I am a dry tree” (Isaiah 56:3). God would not let that name stand. He promised those who held fast his covenant “an everlasting name that shall not be cut off” (Isaiah 56:5). Paul bowed his knees “before the Father, from whom every family in heaven and on earth is named” (Ephesians 3:14–15). Your name is given by your Father, not by your marital status.

Not good to be alone

“It is not good that the man should be alone” (Genesis 2:18). Some read this as meaning that every unmarried person is living in a state God calls “not good.” But the verse shows that we are made for relationship, and God’s first answer was marriage. It is not his only answer. Jesus was unmarried, yet he was not alone in that sense: he lived in deep fellowship with his Father and with his friends. God’s fuller answer to human aloneness is a people, his church, in which the unmarried are brothers, sisters, mothers and fathers.

A retired teacher, never married, once told a younger single friend that for years he had treated his life as a rough draft, waiting for the real version to begin with a wedding. In his forties he realised this was the real version, and Christ was writing it. He did not stop wishing things had been different. But he started living the life he had.

For reflection

What difference does it make to you that Jesus lived his whole earthly life unmarried? What names, spoken or unspoken, have you carried because of your marital status? How does Colossians 2:9–10 answer them? What would it look like to live the life you have, not the one you are waiting for?

2.title: A Gift, Not a Rank
2.essay:
First Corinthians 7 is the chapter in which Scripture speaks most directly about singleness. Read as a whole, it guards against two opposite errors: making singleness superior, and making marriage an idol.

A church with two problems

The Corinthians had written to Paul, and he quotes a line from their letter: “It is good for a man not to have sexual relations with a woman” (1 Corinthians 7:1). Some of them seem to have thought that sex, even in marriage, was unspiritual. Others, as chapter 6 shows, were careless about sexual sin. Paul answers both, telling married couples not to deprive one another (1 Corinthians 7:5) and honouring singleness without despising marriage.

Each has his own gift

“I wish that all were as I myself am. But each has his own gift from God, one of one kind and one of another” (1 Corinthians 7:7). Paul’s word for “gift” is his word for gifts of grace.

Christians read this verse in two main ways. Some hold that the “gift” of singleness is a special ability, given to some, to live contentedly without marriage and without being troubled by strong sexual desire. On this view, those who lack it should normally seek to marry, since Paul says, “if they cannot exercise self-control, they should marry. For it is better to marry than to burn with passion” (1 Corinthians 7:9). As Jesus said, “Not everyone can receive this saying, but only those to whom it is given” (Matthew 19:11).

Others hold that the gift is the state itself. Whatever condition God has assigned for now, single or married, is his gift, and with it he gives the grace to live it. They point to Paul’s rule: “let each person lead the life that the Lord has assigned to him, and to which God has called him” (1 Corinthians 7:17). On this view a single person who longs to marry has not “missed” the gift.

This commentary’s view: singleness and marriage are both gifts, and neither is holier. The state God has given you now is his gift for now, and his grace comes with it. Yet the first view rightly hears Paul’s realism. Strong desire for marriage is not a sign of spiritual failure, and where it is strong, seeking marriage is wise and honourable: “if you do marry, you have not sinned” (1 Corinthians 7:28). The gift is not a verdict on your future. It is grace for today.

Undivided devotion

Paul goes on: “The unmarried man is anxious about the things of the Lord, how to please the Lord. But the married man is anxious about worldly things, how to please his wife, and his interests are divided” (1 Corinthians 7:32–34). He is not saying married people are less spiritual. He is describing availability. A single person often has more freedom of time, place and attention.

And notice his purpose: “I say this for your own benefit, not to lay any restraint upon you, but to promote good order and to secure your undivided devotion to the Lord” (1 Corinthians 7:35). Singleness is not a cage. It is an opportunity. It can be wasted on career or comfort, as marriage can. But it can be poured out: in friendship, hospitality, mission and prayer.

Living lightly

Paul sets all this against the shortness of time. “From now on, let those who have wives live as though they had none … For the present form of this world is passing away” (1 Corinthians 7:29–31). Every believer is to hold this world’s arrangements loosely. Marriage belongs to an age that is ending.

Not a higher rank

For centuries Roman Catholic teaching has held consecrated virginity to be a more excellent state than marriage, while still counting marriage holy. The Reformers rejected that ranking, and they rejected compulsory celibacy for ministers. Paul does say that the one who refrains from marriage “will do even better” (1 Corinthians 7:38), but he says it in view of “the present distress” (1 Corinthians 7:26) and the troubles marriage brings, not as a ladder of holiness. No one is closer to God for being single.

Not an idol either

Many churches today make the opposite error. Marriage is treated as the mark of adulthood, the reward for purity, the place where real life begins. That is an idol, and like every idol it crushes. It tells single people they are behind, and it loads marriage with hopes no spouse can carry. Paul could even say of a widow, “in my judgment she is happier if she remains as she is” (1 Corinthians 7:40). Neither state saves. Christ does.

Seeking marriage is good, and those who do so may pray and take sensible steps. Scripture’s one firm rule is that a believer marries “only in the Lord” (1 Corinthians 7:39). The study Faith for Young Adults says more about choosing and dating well.

A woman in her thirties had been told many times that she would meet someone once she was content. She began to treat contentment as a test she kept failing. A wise older friend showed her that Paul never makes contentment a price for marriage. Contentment is a gift of grace in itself. She still hopes to marry. But she has stopped trying to earn it.

For reflection

Have you tended to think of singleness as a higher calling, or as second best? How does 1 Corinthians 7:7 correct both? What does “undivided devotion” (1 Corinthians 7:35) look like in your present circumstances? Where might your church have made marriage an idol without meaning to?

3.title: Longing, Loneliness and Lament
3.essay:
“Hope deferred makes the heart sick, but a desire fulfilled is a tree of life” (Proverbs 13:12). Scripture knows how it feels to want something good for a long time and not receive it. It does not tell the sick heart to pretend. It teaches it to pray.

Longing is not sin

The desire for a husband or wife, for children, for touch, for someone who knows you and chooses you, is a good desire. God made us for relationship. Longing for marriage is not a lack of faith, nor a sign that Christ is not enough. It becomes sinful only when it rules the heart or turns bitter against God. The psalmist could say, “O Lord, all my longing is before you; my sighing is not hidden from you” (Psalm 38:9). God already sees. You may as well tell him.

The shapes of loneliness

Married people can be lonely too. But singleness has its own shapes of loneliness. Coming home to an empty house. Having no one to tell the small news of the day. Being ill with no one to bring a drink. Weddings, christenings and family holidays. A seat at church between two couples. The question, kindly meant, “Still no one special?” For the widowed it may be the empty side of the bed after decades. For the divorced it may be the wound of having been rejected by the one who promised to stay.

David prayed, “Turn to me and be gracious to me, for I am lonely and afflicted” (Psalm 25:16). Another psalmist wrote, “I lie awake; I am like a lonely sparrow on the housetop” (Psalm 102:7).

Learning to lament

Lament is honest prayer to God about pain. Psalm 13 is a pattern. It begins with complaint: “How long, O LORD? Will you forget me forever? How long will you hide your face from me?” (Psalm 13:1). It moves to request: “Consider and answer me, O LORD my God” (Psalm 13:3). And it ends in trust: “But I have trusted in your steadfast love; my heart shall rejoice in your salvation” (Psalm 13:5). The trust does not cancel the complaint.

Hiding in a cave, David prayed, “Look to the right and see: there is none who takes notice of me; no refuge remains to me; no one cares for my soul” (Psalm 142:4). Then: “You are my refuge, my portion in the land of the living” (Psalm 142:5). And Psalm 88 ends with no resolution at all: “my companions have become darkness” (Psalm 88:18). God placed even that prayer in his book, so that no night is too dark to bring to him. “Trust in him at all times, O people; pour out your heart before him” (Psalm 62:8).

A Saviour who knows

In Gethsemane Jesus said to his closest friends, “My soul is very sorrowful, even to death; remain here, and watch with me” (Matthew 26:38). They fell asleep. “So, could you not watch with me one hour?” (Matthew 26:40). He was “a man of sorrows and acquainted with grief” (Isaiah 53:3). So we have a high priest who is not “unable to sympathize with our weaknesses” (Hebrews 4:15). When you are lonely, you are not praying to someone who has never been alone.

Promises rightly heard

Single people are often handed verses as guarantees of marriage. “Delight yourself in the LORD, and he will give you the desires of your heart” (Psalm 37:4). This is not a formula for getting a spouse. Delighting in the Lord reshapes our desires, until he himself becomes the chief of them, and then he never fails to give it. “No good thing does he withhold from those who walk uprightly” (Psalm 84:11). But God decides what is good, and he has already proved his goodness: “He who did not spare his own Son but gave him up for us all, how will he not also with him graciously give us all things?” (Romans 8:32). A Father who gave his Son is not withholding marriage out of carelessness.

Waiting with hope

The writer of Lamentations, among the ruins of Jerusalem, could still say, “‘The LORD is my portion,’ says my soul, ‘therefore I will hope in him’” (Lamentations 3:24). Paul tells us that all believers “groan inwardly as we wait eagerly for adoption as sons, the redemption of our bodies” (Romans 8:23). Groaning and hoping belong together.

When the darkness deepens

Loneliness can slide into depression. If you find yourself in a darkness that will not lift, see a doctor. Medicine and counselling are no failure of faith. And if you ever think of ending your life, tell someone at once: call the emergency services or a crisis line, or go to a trusted person now. You are not a burden. Your life is precious to God and to his people.

A man in his forties drove home alone after his younger brother’s wedding. He had smiled all day. In the car he prayed Psalm 13 aloud, word for word, and wept. But the next week he told a friend from church how the day had really been, and the friend began calling him every Sunday evening. It helped.

For reflection

Which shapes of loneliness are most familiar to you? Try writing your own lament, following the pattern of Psalm 13: complaint, request, trust. How should Psalm 37:4 and Romans 8:32 be heard by someone who longs to marry? If you are married, how could you “weep with those who weep” (Romans 12:15) with a single friend this month?

4.title: Faithful in Body, Content in Heart
4.essay:
For most single Christians the call to sexual faithfulness is not a theory. It is daily, and it is often hard. This chapter is written not to shame anyone but to strengthen the weary.

Your body is not on hold

Single people sometimes feel their bodies are on hold until marriage. Scripture disagrees. “Your body is a temple of the Holy Spirit within you … You are not your own, for you were bought with a price. So glorify God in your body” (1 Corinthians 6:19–20). The single body belongs to Christ now, and it glorifies him now. “For this is the will of God, your sanctification: that you abstain from sexual immorality” (1 Thessalonians 4:3). That is not a special rule for singles. It is God’s will for every believer.

Desire is not the enemy

Sexual desire is part of God’s good creation, not something shameful in itself. Paul was realistic about how strong it can be (1 Corinthians 7:9). Feeling desire, or feeling tempted, is not sin. Jesus “in every respect has been tempted as we are, yet without sin” (Hebrews 4:15). The question is what we do with desire: whether we feed it, indulge it in fantasy, or bring it to God and direct it rightly.

Jesus did set the standard at the level of the heart: “everyone who looks at a woman with lustful intent has already committed adultery with her in his heart” (Matthew 5:28). That rules out pornography, which today is the most common snare for single Christians, women as well as men. But he said it not to crush us, but so that we would stop pretending and come to him for mercy.

Grace that trains

The power for purity is not fear but grace. “For the grace of God has appeared, bringing salvation for all people, training us to renounce ungodliness and worldly passions, and to live self-controlled, upright, and godly lives in the present age” (Titus 2:11–12). The same grace that forgives also trains. And “God is faithful, and he will not let you be tempted beyond your ability, but with the temptation he will also provide the way of escape” (1 Corinthians 10:13).

That way of escape is often very practical. Do not fight alone: tell one or two trusted Christians of your own sex what you struggle with. Notice when you are most vulnerable, often when tired, lonely, bored or late at night, and plan for those hours. Put guards on your devices. Look after your body with sleep and exercise. Fill your life with friendship, service and work that matters. Purity is not only saying no. It is a life so full of better things that sin has less room.

When you fall

Many single Christians carry a secret history of failure, and shame keeps them hidden. Hear the gospel: “If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness” (1 John 1:9). You are not your worst moment. Confess it, receive his cleansing, and get up again. A thousand restarts in the strength of grace are better than one proud pretence.

Same-sex attracted believers

Some Christians experience attraction to their own sex. This commentary holds the historic view, held with compassion: same-sex sexual relationships are contrary to God’s will. For many such believers, faithfulness to Christ will mean a single life, sometimes for life. That is a costly obedience, and those who walk it deserve honour, not suspicion. Their longing for intimacy and belonging is a good human longing. It can be met, in deep measure if not in every way, through close and godly friendships and through a church that lives as real family. A church that asks such costly faithfulness must also give what Jesus promised: brothers, sisters, mothers and homes (Mark 10:30). The study Biblical Sexuality treats these questions more fully.

Content while longing

Paul wrote, “I have learned the secret of facing plenty and hunger, abundance and need. I can do all things through him who strengthens me” (Philippians 4:12–13). Contentment is learned, slowly. It is not pretending you have no longings. It is finding that Christ is enough even while the longing remains. Both can live in the same heart. “But godliness with contentment is great gain” (1 Timothy 6:6).

The psalmist, far from comfort, wrote, “O God, you are my God; earnestly I seek you; my soul thirsts for you … Because your steadfast love is better than life, my lips will praise you” (Psalm 63:1–3). That is the secret. The God who made our desires is himself the deepest object of them. Every good longing, for love and for being fully known, is at bottom a longing for him.

A woman in her late twenties had struggled with pornography since her teens. She thought it was a man’s problem and that she must be unusually wicked. At last she told an older woman in her church, who did not flinch. They prayed together, set some practical guards in place, and met every fortnight. She still has hard nights. But she is no longer hiding, and she has found that Christ’s mercy is larger than her shame.

For reflection

How does knowing that your body belongs to Christ now shape how you live? Who could you be honest with about your struggles? How does Titus 2:11–12 change the motive for purity? What would it mean for you to be content while still longing?

5.title: Widowed and Single Again
5.essay:
Some people never expected to be single again. They stood at the graveside of a husband or wife, or watched a marriage end against their will. When Naomi came home to Bethlehem a widow, having buried her sons too, she said, “Do not call me Naomi; call me Mara, for the Almighty has dealt very bitterly with me. I went away full, and the LORD has brought me back empty” (Ruth 1:20–21).

The God of the widow

From the law onwards God names himself as the widow’s protector. “He executes justice for the fatherless and the widow, and loves the sojourner” (Deuteronomy 10:18). “The LORD watches over the sojourners; he upholds the widow and the fatherless” (Psalm 146:9).

Jesus showed the same heart. Near the town of Nain he met a funeral: “the only son of his mother, and she was a widow” (Luke 7:12). And “when the Lord saw her, he had compassion on her” (Luke 7:13). He raised her son and gave him back to her. Even from the cross he provided for his own mother, by then, it seems, a widow, entrusting her to John: “And from that hour the disciple took her to his own home” (John 19:27).

Naomi and Ruth

The book of Ruth begins with three widows. Naomi calls herself bitter and empty, and Scripture records her words without rebuke. Ruth, her widowed daughter-in-law, refuses to leave her: “where you go I will go, and where you lodge I will lodge. Your people shall be my people, and your God my God” (Ruth 1:16).

Quietly, God works. Ruth gleans in the field of Boaz, who blesses her as one who has come to take refuge under the Lord’s wings (Ruth 2:12). In the end Ruth marries again, and the women of Bethlehem say to Naomi that the child “shall be to you a restorer of life and a nourisher of your old age” (Ruth 4:15). Naomi never remarries, yet she too is restored, in a family she had not expected. And that child, Obed, was the grandfather of David, from whose line Christ would come. God’s restoration does not always mean remarriage. But he does not leave his widows empty.

Anna

Anna was married for seven years and then lived “as a widow until she was eighty-four. She did not depart from the temple, worshiping with fasting and prayer night and day” (Luke 2:37). Her long widowhood was not wasted. She was among the first to see the infant Christ, and she spoke of him “to all who were waiting for the redemption of Jerusalem” (Luke 2:38).

The church and its widows

The early church took widows seriously. When some were neglected, the apostles appointed men to put it right (Acts 6:1–6). In Joppa, when Dorcas died, “all the widows stood beside him weeping and showing tunics and other garments that Dorcas made while she was with them” (Acts 9:39).

Paul writes to Timothy, “Honor widows who are truly widows” (1 Timothy 5:3). Families come first: children and grandchildren should care for their widowed parents (1 Timothy 5:4, 8). The church supports those left without family, the widow who is “left all alone, has set her hope on God and continues in supplications and prayers night and day” (1 Timothy 5:5). Older widows of godly character could be “enrolled” (1 Timothy 5:9), it seems in a recognised ministry of prayer and service. Paul’s caution about younger widows (1 Timothy 5:11–15) is not disdain for remarriage. He actually encourages them to marry. His concern is that they should not make a pledge they might later break, or drift into idleness.

Freedom to remarry, and freedom not to

A widow “is free to be married to whom she wishes, only in the Lord” (1 Corinthians 7:39), and the same holds for a widower. Remarriage is no betrayal of the one who died. Neither is remaining single a failure to move on. No one should be hurried or made to feel guilty either way. Widowers need particular care: many men are more isolated after a wife’s death than they expected.

Divorced and separated

For the divorced, the loss is different. The former spouse is still living, and there may be rejection, betrayal and lasting conflict, sometimes over children. Some are free to remarry; some, Scripture says, should seek reconciliation. The study Divorce & Remarriage sets this out carefully. But whatever the circumstances, the divorced are not second-class members of Christ’s church. And anyone who has left a home because of abuse should know that safety comes first, that abuse must be reported to the authorities, and that leaving to escape it is not the separation Paul forbids.

Single parents carry a double load. God sees them, and his church must see them too, with meals, lifts, help with children and simple friendship.

A man of seventy-four lost his wife after forty-eight years of marriage. The evenings were silent. A young family in his church began inviting him every Thursday. He mended their children’s bicycles, and they taught him to make a simple soup. Two years on he still misses his wife every day. But he has a place at a table again.

For reflection

What does God’s repeated care for widows in Scripture tell you about him? How does Naomi’s story show that restoration need not mean remarriage? Who in your church is widowed, divorced or raising children alone, and what could you do for them this month? If you are single again, which part of this chapter speaks most to you?

6.title: A Family Now, a Wedding to Come
6.essay:
Peter once said to Jesus, “See, we have left everything and followed you” (Mark 10:28). Jesus answered with a promise that every single Christian should know by heart, and that every church is called to help keep.

A hundredfold now

“Truly, I say to you, there is no one who has left house or brothers or sisters or mother or father or children or lands, for my sake and for the gospel, who will not receive a hundredfold now in this time, houses and brothers and sisters and mothers and children and lands, with persecutions, and in the age to come eternal life” (Mark 10:29–30). Notice the words “now in this time.” Jesus does not only promise heaven. He promises a family here, a hundred times larger than the one given up. And he keeps that promise through his people.

Paul knew it. “Greet Rufus, chosen in the Lord; also his mother, who has been a mother to me as well” (Romans 16:13). The single apostle had a mother in the faith. He told Timothy to treat “older women as mothers, younger women as sisters, in all purity” (1 Timothy 5:2). At the cross, a new household was formed when Jesus gave his mother to John, and John took her into his home (John 19:26–27). In the church, family is not only made by marriage and birth. It is made by the blood of Christ.

What this looks like

A church that believes Mark 10:30 will look different. Its homes will be open, not only for a polite dinner but for ordinary life: Sunday lunch, the school run, the washing up, Christmas morning. Single people will be welcomed as part of the household, not as guests to be entertained. It will notice who is ill and alone, who has no one to call in an emergency, who is growing old without children to look after them, and it will make plans together. Its preaching will not assume that everyone is married, and its leadership will not sideline single men and women.

Single people are not only receivers in this family. They are often its great givers. Single Christians can open their own homes and “seek to show hospitality” (Romans 12:13). They can be aunts and uncles to other people’s children, mentors to the young and companions to the old. All can “do good to everyone, and especially to those who are of the household of faith” (Galatians 6:10). The study Friendship & Hospitality says more about how.

The Bridegroom is waiting

There is something more wonderful still. Jesus called himself the Bridegroom. “Can the wedding guests fast while the bridegroom is with them?” (Mark 2:19). But the Bridegroom has not yet had his wedding. At the Last Supper he said, “I tell you I will not drink again of this fruit of the vine until that day when I drink it new with you in my Father’s kingdom” (Matthew 26:29).

So the single Saviour is also waiting for his wedding day. Every single Christian who waits, hopes and longs is waiting alongside him. And every believer, married or single, is already betrothed. Paul told the Corinthians, “I betrothed you to one husband, to present you as a pure virgin to Christ” (2 Corinthians 11:2). The deepest marriage of your life is not behind you, and it is not uncertain. It is ahead, and it is sure.

When marriage gives way

Jesus said, “For in the resurrection they neither marry nor are given in marriage” (Matthew 22:30). Human marriage, good as it is, is a signpost. When we arrive, the sign is no longer needed. The never-married will not have missed the one thing that mattered. No one will sit at that table as a single among couples. All will be the one Bride.

John saw it: “the holy city, new Jerusalem, coming down out of heaven from God, prepared as a bride adorned for her husband” (Revelation 21:2). And he heard the promise that answers every lonely night: “He will wipe away every tear from their eyes, and death shall be no more, neither shall there be mourning, nor crying, nor pain anymore” (Revelation 21:4). The crowd that sings at the marriage of the Lamb cries, “Hallelujah! For the Lord our God the Almighty reigns” (Revelation 19:6).

Until then, nothing can part a single believer from the love of their Bridegroom. Neither “things present nor things to come … will be able to separate us from the love of God in Christ Jesus our Lord” (Romans 8:38–39).

A small church realised that one of its oldest members, a woman who had never married, had no living relatives at all. Two families and a younger single man met with her and drew up a simple plan: who would visit, who would drive her to appointments, who would be called if she went into hospital. When she died some years later, the church was there, as family, at the end. At her funeral they sang of the marriage supper of the Lamb.

For reflection

How has the church been, or failed to be, the “hundredfold” family of Mark 10:30 for you? What is one practical step your household could take to welcome a single person as family? How does knowing that Christ himself is waiting for his wedding change how you see your own waiting? What do you look forward to most at the marriage supper of the Lamb?
